records.text: Two days after surgery, remove the mastoid dressing, or head bandage. Next, check whether tape covers the incision, or surgical cut, behind the ear.
If there is tape, keep the area dry until three days after surgery. Do not clean the incision before that time.

If there is no tape, clean the edges of the incision gently twice a day. Use a mix of equal parts hydrogen peroxide and distilled water. Then apply an over-the-counter antibiotic ointment, such as bacitracin.
Three days after surgery, you may shower and wash your hair.
Your wound check and ear exam are about two weeks after surgery. The stitches dissolve, so they do not need to be removed.
Call your surgeon or clinic staff if all three signs below are present. The incision is red and swollen. It does not get better over the next one to two days. It hurts when touched.
Call if you have a fever above 101.5 degrees Fahrenheit.
Call if the skin behind your ear is swollen or feels like fluid is building up under it.
Call if you have a headache, light sensitivity, or excessive lethargy.
Call if you have a wound-care question or another medical concern about you or your child.

For routine questions for the clinic or surgeon, leave a message on the nursing line at 415-353-2148. The UCSF page says you should get a call within 12 hours. If no one calls, call again. For an emergency, call 415-476-1000 and ask for the Otolaryngology resident on call.

Two days after surgery, remove the head bandage. Then check: is there tape over the incision behind your ear?

If there is tape — keep the area dry until three days after surgery, and do not clean it before then. If there is no tape — clean the edges gently twice a day with equal parts hydrogen peroxide and distilled water, then apply an antibiotic ointment such as bacitracin.
Three days after surgery, you may shower and wash your hair. Your wound check and ear exam are about two weeks after surgery — the stitches dissolve on their own.
Call your surgeon or clinic if all three of these are true: the incision is red and swollen, it is not getting better over one to two days, and it hurts when touched.

Also call for any of these: a fever above 101.5 degrees Fahrenheit; swelling, or fluid building up, behind your ear; a headache, light sensitivity, or excessive lethargy; or any question or concern about you or your child.

For routine questions, leave a message on the nursing line: 415-353-2148. You should get a call back within 12 hours — if no one calls, call again. For an emergency, call 415-476-1000 and ask for the Otolaryngology resident on call.
